payload.prompt: Probability that this company files for bankruptcy (Chapter 11 or Chapter 7) within 24 months of this filing date?
payload.context:
10-K for the fiscal year ended November 30, 2007, filed January 29, 2008. Figures hand-transcribed from the filing (pre-XBRL).
- Net revenues: $19,257M, a record, up from $17,583M; fourth consecutive record year.
- Net income: $4,192M, also a record (prior years: $4,007M, $3,260M).
- Total revenues $59,003M less interest expense $39,746M: most gross revenue is recycled into funding costs.
- Total assets: $691,063M, up 37% in one year (from $503,545M; $410,063M two years ago).
- Total stockholders' equity: $22,490M. Assets are roughly 30.7x equity.
- Long-term borrowings: $123,150M, up from $81,178M; the balance of the footings is funded short-term (repo, commercial paper, payables).
- The firm carries large inventories of mortgages and mortgage-backed securities; residential mortgage originations were a major business through mid-2007.
- Credit ratings: single-A range, stable at filing.

answer_key.resolution: Lehman Brothers Holdings filed for Chapter 11 on September 15, 2008 — about 7.5 months after this 10-K was filed, well inside the 24-month window. The record FY2007 earnings were real under GAAP, but the balance sheet was 30.7x levered and funded overnight against assets (mortgages, CMBS) whose value was already falling. Base-rate note: roughly 1-3% of listed companies enter bankruptcy within any 24-month window, but a 30x-levered wholesale-funded balance sheet in a deteriorating asset class sits far above that class rate.
answer_key.source: 8-K Item 1.03 filed 2008-09-19, accession 0001104659-08-059632 (CIK 806085). As-of figures from the FY2007 10-K, accession 0001104659-08-005476.

hints.text: Divide total assets by total equity, then ask what happens to that structure if asset values fall three percent.

explanation: The income statement said record year; the balance sheet said one bad quarter from the end. At 30.7x leverage, a 3.3% decline in asset values wipes out equity entirely, and most of the funding rolled overnight. The lesson is that for a leveraged financial, earnings are noise and the liability structure is signal. You were not asked whether management was smart or the franchise valuable — only whether a 30x-levered mortgage-heavy book funded short could survive two years of a housing bust. A forecast well above the 2% class base rate was warranted; certainty was not, since Bear Stearns was rescued rather than liquidated only weeks after this filing.

answer_key.resolution: No bankruptcy, no going-concern disclosure. Tesla paid the $920M converts at maturity in March 2019, raised roughly $2.7B of new equity and converts in May 2019, and was solidly profitable by late 2020. EDGAR shows no 8-K Item 1.03 and no Item 4.02 in the window ending February 19, 2021. answer_key.source: Absence of 8-K Items 1.03/4.02 for CIK 1318605 between 2019-02-19 and 2021-02-19 (EDGAR submissions index). As-of figures from the FY2018 10-K, accession 0001564590-19-003165.

hints.text: The headline is a $976M loss. What direction is operating cash flow moving, and does it cover capex yet?

explanation: The narrative said death watch; the cash flow statement said inflection. Operating cash flow swung from negative to +$2.1B and now covered capex, the two most recent quarters were GAAP-profitable, and cash on hand covered the near-term converts four times over. Companies with positive and improving operating cash flow rarely file within two years — that combination sits below the already-low base rate, not above it. The discipline being trained: separate how loudly a company is argued about from what its cash generation says. A calibrated answer here was low single digits, not the 30-50% the headlines implied.

When a reporting unit deteriorates while its carrying value grows, the annual impairment test becomes a countdown, not a formality. You should have been far above the 7% class rate here — 40-60% was defensible.

Going-concern language appears in well under 5% of large-company 10-Ks, and among those that also have negative equity and no core business improving, two-year survival is the exception. The only argument for restraint was the controlling shareholder's willingness to keep lending, which bought time but not solvency. A forecast in the 50-70% range was calibrated; 2% would have been base-rate worship.

payload.company_label: a subscription video service pivoting from discs to streaming

answer_key.resolution: No restatement and no Item 4.02 ever came. EDGAR shows no 8-K Item 4.02 for Netflix between February 2012 and February 2014 (nor since related to this period). The content-amortization estimates that short sellers attacked were aggressive-looking but defensible judgments, disclosed in the accounting-policy and commitments notes, and the SEC never required a revision of them. Base-rate note: only about 2-4% of filers issue a 4.02 non-reliance within two years, and disagreeing with a disclosed estimate is not an accounting error.
answer_key.source: Absence of 8-K Item 4.02 for CIK 1065280, 2012-02-10 through 2014-02-10 (EDGAR submissions index). As-of figures from the FY2011 10-K, accession 0001193125-12-053009.

hints.text: A restatement requires an error under GAAP. Is slow content amortization an error, or a disclosed estimate you happen to dislike?

explanation: The trap is conflating an aggressive estimate with a misstatement. Content amortization pace was fully disclosed, consistently applied, and a matter of judgment — the kind of thing analysts argue about and restatements almost never touch. Restatements come from errors and control failures: misapplied standards, fabricated entries, arithmetic that fails. Nothing in this filing pointed there; the company's problems (subscriber backlash, off-balance-sheet content commitments) were business risks in plain sight, not concealed ones. When the bear case is 'I disagree with a disclosed estimate,' stay near the 3% base rate. The off-balance-sheet commitments were the real reading lesson — and they argued for equity risk, not restatement risk.

The exposure was structural — net income of $346M sitting on top of a multi-billion-dollar depreciation expense governed by residual-value estimates, meaning a one-percent tweak to fleet depreciation could move earnings double digits. Add an unabsorbed mega-acquisition, a headquarters move that gutted the accounting staff, and a spin-off in flight, and you have the classic preconditions for control failure. Those conditions justified nudging above the 3% base rate — to perhaps 8-12% — not to 50%. Hindsight items score calibration, and this one punishes both the player who saw nothing and the one who claims they saw everything.

payload.prompt: Probability that this company files for bankruptcy within 24 months of this filing date?

answer_key.resolution: PG&E filed for Chapter 11 on January 29, 2019 — less than a year after this filing. The 2017 fire liabilities were still unresolved when the November 2018 Camp Fire, ignited by PG&E equipment, became the deadliest fire in California history and pushed estimated liabilities beyond $30B. The bankruptcy was a liability event, not an operating one: the utility kept earning regulated returns throughout. Base-rate note: utilities file at far below the 1-3% general rate — which is exactly why the unbounded, non-estimable contingency plus a suspended dividend deserved most of the weight here.
answer_key.source: 8-K Item 1.03 filed 2019-01-29, accession 0001193125-19-019657; preceding 8-K of 2019-01-14 (accession 0000950157-19-000032) giving the required 15-day notice (CIK 1004980). As-of figures from the FY2017 10-K, accession 0001004980-18-000003.

hints.text: The income statement is the calmest page in this filing. Read the contingencies note and the dividend decision together.

explanation: Every conventional metric said sleep well: monopoly revenues, $6B of operating cash flow, investment-grade paper. The danger lived entirely in the notes — an unquantifiable legal doctrine that converts acts of nature into corporate liabilities, attached to a service territory that burns annually. The board telegraphed its own probability estimate by suspending the dividend; boards of healthy utilities do not do that. This is the boring-company-that-blew-up case: the statements measured the past, the contingency note described the exposure, and the exposure was unbounded. A calibrated answer was meaningfully above the class base rate — 10-25% — while still acknowledging that the catastrophic second fire was not foreseeable as a certainty.

answer_key.resolution: Frontier filed for Chapter 11 on April 14, 2020 — about 13.5 months after this filing — to restructure more than $10B of its debt. The mechanics were exactly as the coverage ratio implied: a melting revenue base could not both service $1.5B of annual interest and fund the network investment needed to stop the melting. Base-rate note: the 1-3% two-year class rate applies to healthy filers; sub-1x EBIT interest coverage with negative-trending revenue and serial impairments of the acquired asset base defines the high-risk subset.
answer_key.source: 8-K Item 1.03 filed 2020-04-15, accession 0001140361-20-008876 (petition date 2020-04-14, CIK 20520). As-of figures from the FY2018 10-K, accession 0000020520-19-000005.

hints.text: Compare operating income to interest expense, then ask which direction the numerator is trending.

explanation: One ratio carried this case: operating income of $827M against interest of $1,536M — 0.54x coverage — with the numerator shrinking every single quarter. The serial goodwill impairments were the accounting system's own confession that the acquired subscriber base was worth less than what was borrowed to buy it. Positive operating cash flow ($1.8B) is the number that fools people here; it looks like solvency until you notice it cannot cover interest plus the capex a network business cannot skip. When coverage is below 1x and the trend is down, bankruptcy stops being a tail event and becomes the base case — 30-50% was a calibrated answer.

payload.prompt: Probability that this company files for bankruptcy within 36 months of this filing date?
payload.context:
10-K for the fiscal year ended December 26, 2015, filed February 18, 2016. Figures as reported in that filing.
- Revenue: $3,991M, down 28% from $5,506M ($5,299M two years ago), as its larger rival dominates the core processor market.
- Net loss: $660M (prior years: −$403M, −$83M) — losses in each of the last four quarters.
- Gross margin: 27% ($1,080M gross profit) — thin for a chip designer.
- Operating loss: $481M.
- Operating cash flow: negative $226M, the third consecutive negative year (−$98M, −$148M).
- Cash: $785M. Long-term debt: $2,025M, with major maturities in 2019-2020 but little due before then.
- Stockholders' equity: negative $412M (down from +$187M).
- The company has outsourced its factories, cut costs repeatedly, and is betting on a new processor architecture and semi-custom game-console chips it says will ship in 2016-2017.

answer_key.resolution: No bankruptcy. EDGAR shows no 8-K Item 1.03 for AMD in the window ending February 18, 2019. The Zen architecture launched in 2017 as Ryzen and EPYC, revenue returned to growth, and by the end of the window AMD had refinanced its debt and its stock had risen several-fold. Base-rate note: about 2-4% of listed firms file within three years; AMD's losses argued for more, but its liquidity runway (cash roughly covering cumulative burn, no meaningful maturities inside the window) and fab-light cost structure argued the timing risk was past the window.
answer_key.source: Absence of 8-K Item 1.03 for CIK 2488, 2016-02-18 through 2019-02-18 (EDGAR submissions index). As-of figures from the FY2015 10-K, accession 0000002488-16-000111.

hints.text: Negative equity is a stock measure. Bankruptcy timing runs on flows: cash, burn rate, and the maturity wall.

explanation: Negative equity frightens; maturities kill. AMD's book equity was below zero — an accounting residue of accumulated losses — but $785M of cash against roughly $200M of annual burn gave it about three years of runway, and the debt wall sat in 2019-2020, at the far edge of the window. Asset-light chip designers can also shrink costs faster than asset-heavy manufacturers. That made this a solvency question about timing, and the timing favored survival even if the turnaround bet failed. The calibrated answer was elevated but restrained — 10-20% — and the case pairs deliberately with the telecom in this set, where the same class of question had coverage below 1x and no product-cycle option value. Ugly is not the same as due.

payload.prompt: Probability that, within five years of this filing date, the SEC brings an enforcement action against this company concerning its disclosures about how it achieved its revenue results in this period?
payload.context:
10-K for fiscal year 2016, filed February 23, 2017. Figures as reported in that filing.
- Net revenues: $4,825M, up 22% from $3,963M — but growth decelerated sharply in the fourth quarter, ending a long public streak of 20%-plus growth quarters that management had repeatedly emphasized.
- Net income: $257M (prior year: $233M). Operating income: $417M versus $409M — margin compressed from 10.3% to 8.7%.
- Accounts receivable: $623M, up 44% from $434M — receivables growing twice as fast as revenue.
- Inventory: $917M, up 17% from $783M.
- Operating cash flow: $304M (prior year: negative $44M).
- Total assets: $3,644M; stockholders' equity: $2,031M.
- The growth narrative is the stock's entire valuation case, and management guides to it explicitly.

answer_key.resolution: On May 3, 2021 — about 4.2 years after this filing — Under Armour announced a settled SEC action over its disclosures concerning "pull forward" sales from the third quarter of 2015 through the fourth quarter of 2016: the SEC's order found it had accelerated roughly $408M of orders into earlier quarters to meet revenue expectations without disclosing that practice, and the company paid a $9.0M civil penalty, neither admitting nor denying the findings. There was no restatement and no fraud finding against the company; the case was about undisclosed practices behind the growth streak. Base-rate note: SEC enforcement over a given filer's revenue disclosures runs low single digits over five years; a receivables-revenue divergence during a publicly defended growth streak is the classic elevated-risk pattern.
answer_key.source: Under Armour 8-K Item 8.01 filed 2021-05-03, accession 0001336917-21-000021, announcing the settled SEC action and $9.0M penalty regarding pull-forward sales Q3 2015-Q4 2016. As-of figures from the FY2016 10-K, accession 0001336917-17-000017.

hints.text: Revenue grew 22%. What grew 44%, and what does that gap usually mean about when the revenue was booked?

explanation: Receivables up 44% against revenue up 22% means, mechanically, that an outsized share of the year's sales were booked near quarter-ends and remained uncollected — precisely the footprint that order acceleration leaves. Add the motive: a management team publicly defending a 20%-plus growth streak that was visibly dying in Q4. What the SEC ultimately established was narrower than fraud — undisclosed pull-forwards that made the streak look organic — and note that the accounting itself was not restated; the sales were real, just borrowed from the future without telling anyone. The reading lesson is that receivables drift plus a narrative under pressure elevates disclosure risk specifically, and the honest forecast was several times the base rate but still modest: 10-20%.

payload.prompt: Probability that this company files for bankruptcy within 24 months of this filing date?
payload.context:
10-K for fiscal year 2019, filed February 25, 2020. Figures as reported in that filing.
- Revenues: $9,779M — a record year, up from $9,504M and $8,803M.
- Net loss: $58M, the smallest in years (prior: −$225M; +$327M in 2017) — the turnaround narrative is that the company has stabilized.
- Operating cash flow: $2,900M, up from $2,556M.
- Cash: $865M. Total assets: $24,627M; stockholders' equity: $1,769M.
- Total debt: $17,089M — $13,368M of vehicle debt plus $3,721M of non-vehicle debt.
- The vehicle debt is securitized: the fleet itself is the collateral, and the structures require the company to top up collateral if used-vehicle values fall, on roughly a monthly mark.
- Equity is about 7% of assets; the business rents cars at airports, so revenue is tied directly to travel volumes.

answer_key.resolution: Hertz filed for Chapter 11 on May 22, 2020 — less than three months after this filing, among the fastest 10-K-to-bankruptcy sequences on record for a company of its size. COVID-19 collapsed airport travel in March-April 2020, used-car values fell, and the securitized vehicle-debt structures demanded collateral top-ups Hertz could not fund after lessor negotiations failed. Base-rate note: the 1-3% class rate was arguably the right neighborhood on the filing date — the pandemic's severity was not yet knowable on February 25, 2020 — which is what makes this a calibration case rather than a red-flag case.
answer_key.source: 8-K Items 1.01/1.03 filed 2020-05-26, accession 0001104659-20-065674 (petition date 2020-05-22, CIK 1657853). As-of figures from the FY2019 10-K, accession 0001657853-20-000007.

hints.text: Record revenue is the headline. The debt note tells you what happens to the securitized fleet financing if used-car prices drop.

explanation: This is the humbling case: the outcome was true, and yet a low forecast was close to the right forecast. On the filing date the visible facts were record revenue, improving losses, and $2.9B of operating cash flow; the pandemic collapse of air travel was weeks away and not in any filing. What you could see — and should have priced — was fragility rather than distress: 10x leverage on 7% equity, revenue chained to a single demand source (airport traffic), and vehicle debt whose collateral marks turn a used-car price decline into an immediate cash call. Fragile structures deserve a forecast above the base rate even when nothing is currently wrong, because they convert any shock into insolvency. Something like 4-8% was calibrated; both 2% and 40% were errors of different kinds. Under a Brier score, being 'wrong' with an honest 6% on a case like this is how you win over a hundred forecasts.
